problem: Existing surveys on socially-aware robot navigation each cover one angle: social requirements such as comfort, naturalness and cultural conventions (Kruse et al. 2013), or map types such as metric, semantic and social mapping (Charalampous et al. 2017). No survey jointly covers the areas a human-aware robot must combine: active vision, visual robot navigation, human-robot interaction and human behaviour analysis/forecasting.
motivation: Companion, healthcare and assistive robots must move in a socially compliant way before any higher-level interaction can succeed. Yet research is fragmented. Navigation has objective metrics, benchmarks and simulators, while HRI is evaluated subjectively. Activity recognition and trajectory prediction are rarely integrated into navigation, and mainstream simulators (Habitat, AI2-THOR) do not yet support human actors. The authors argue that 'correct' social behaviour requires fusing insights from all four areas.
key_idea: An interdisciplinary survey of image-based human-aware robot navigation. It connects active vision, map-based vs. mapless visual navigation and its benchmark tasks, simulators and datasets, human-robot interaction and proxemics, and human behaviour modelling (pose estimation, activity recognition/forecasting, trajectory prediction). In each area it highlights the works that already implement socially-aware navigation.
insight: Most building blocks for socially-aware navigation already exist in separate communities: RL/IRL navigation, learning from demonstration, fuzzy control, social-force models, activity recognition, trajectory forecasting and photorealistic simulators. They are rarely combined, and socially-aware navigation lacks formal, objective evaluation. The authors therefore suggest decomposing social navigation into well-defined, measurable subtasks, analogous to PointGoal navigation or coverage-based exploration. Examples are human following (with metrics such as percentage of steps with the human in frame, steps at correct distance, and personal-space penalties), handovers, continuous observation, and EQA with a human asking the question. They also recommend adding humans to existing simulators rather than building new ones.
method: Active vision paradigm: contrasts active and passive vision and active perception vs. active learning; argues embodied agents see non-curated, action-dependent input unlike ImageNet/COCO, so movement should be treated as a feature.

Visual robot navigation taxonomy: map-based (metric/occupancy grids, topological maps, SLAM, neural topological SLAM) vs. mapless navigation (RL-based agents that are implicitly mapless, auxiliary tasks). Benchmark tasks covered: PointGoal/ObjectGoal/AreaGoal, exploration (frontier, coverage, uncertainty/occupancy anticipation) and Embodied Question Answering.

Learning paradigms with socially-aware examples: fuzzy logic/control (e.g. hallway if-then rules), reinforcement learning (CADRL-style socially aware motion planning, crowd-robot interaction, IRL), and learning by demonstration (role-playing learning, data-driven HRI, IRL + RRT*). Comparison tables (e.g. Table 1) list problem, algorithm, dataset, metrics and whether real humans were tested.

Simulation-based learning and sim-to-real: realistic simulators (Habitat, Gibson, iGibson, AI2-THOR/RoboTHOR, Replica), learned domain transfer (CycleGAN, SimGAN, domain-invariant content space), pretrain-then-finetune, and domain randomization. Datasets (Matterport3D, Active Vision Dataset) are tabulated separately from frameworks (UnrealCV, MORSE, Gazebo, Habitat, etc.).
Human-robot interaction: social, industrial and healthcare contexts, and proxemics.

Human behaviour analysis: pose estimation, activity recognition, action anticipation, and trajectory prediction (Social LSTM, social force, IRL), with socially-aware navigation works tabulated (Table 7). Also covers trajectory datasets (ETH, UCY, Train Station, Edinburgh Forum, Stanford Drone, PETS 2009) and activity datasets.

Discussion of research gaps: formalised evaluation via subtasks (human following, handover, observation, human-posed EQA), interaction via language (VLN-style), gesture and emotion recognition, and human-populated simulation datasets (Tolani et al., SEAN, VirtualHome, iGibson Challenge 2021 crowds).

setting.observation: surveyed works focus mainly on image-based input (RGB / RGB-D); some distance-sensor works are included for historical influence
setting.simulator: n/a (surveys Habitat, Gibson, iGibson, AI2-THOR/iTHOR/RoboTHOR, Replica, UnrealCV, MORSE, Gazebo, Matterport3D)

numbers_note: Survey paper with no experimental results of its own. Its tables are qualitative comparisons (algorithms, datasets, metrics, real-human tests), not benchmark numbers. The middle part of the text was omitted in the provided extraction.
results: No quantitative results. The survey concludes that few works target socially-aware navigation specifically. Most approaches are confined to navigation without humans, or to HRI without robot movement. Existing simulators could in principle be augmented with humans. Progress is blocked by the lack of formal, objective social-navigation metrics and of human-populated embodied datasets.
limitations: Descriptive survey with no quantitative cross-method comparison or unified benchmark results.

Deliberately restricted to image-based sensing: LiDAR-only trajectory datasets, inertial/RFID activity recognition and direct social interaction (talking, touching, collaboration) are largely excluded.
Written in mid-2021, so it predates human-populated embodied benchmarks such as Habitat 3.0 social navigation and LLM-based navigation methods.
